title: 9% of UK Workers Got No Job Onboarding — Survey
paragraphs: Starting a new job can be exciting, but also stressful. A good onboarding process, which helps new employees learn about their role and their company, can make a big difference. However, a new survey suggests that many workers in the UK are not getting enough support when they start.
The survey was carried out by HBHR, a company that makes software for human resources departments. It asked 1,000 workers in the UK about their experiences of starting new jobs.
The results showed that 9% of workers had received no formal onboarding at all when they started a role. In addition, 12% said they had received little or no formal training for their job.

This lack of support may have serious effects. On average, workers said it took them 7.3 months to feel fully settled and productive in a new role. Around 9% said it took them more than a year, and 7% said they never reached that point. Furthermore, 10% said they had seriously considered quitting within a month of starting a new job, and 9% said they had left a job within the first three months.
Young workers seemed to be the most affected. Onboarding had a negative effect on how 16% of people aged 25 to 35 viewed their employer, compared with only 3% of those aged 45 to 54.

Experts say managers play an important role. Nadia Nagamootoo, the founder of Avenir Consulting, said managers should help new employees feel valued, including through regular check-ins during their first few months. Without proper onboarding, according to Nagamootoo, new workers are left to understand the company's culture on their own.
Simone Robinson of the training company First Ascent Group added that things that seem obvious to long-term employees can be very useful information for newcomers.
A separate poll by the magazine People Management found that 64% of respondents believe support from managers is the most important factor in keeping new employees.
